objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: Which conditions cause a Service Bus message to be moved to the dead-letter queue automatically? Choose three.

options.text: The delivery count exceeds `MaxDeliveryCount`
The message time to live expires
A subscription rule error during evaluation
The receiver calls `AbandonMessageAsync`
The message exceeds the queue's maximum size

explanation: Automatic dead-lettering happens on delivery-count exhaustion, TTL expiry (when dead-lettering on expiration is enabled) and filter evaluation errors. An application can also dead-letter explicitly with `DeadLetterMessageAsync`.

whyWrong.D: Abandon releases the lock and makes the message available again; it increments the delivery count but does not itself dead-letter.
whyWrong.E: An oversized message is rejected at send time with an exception — it never enters the queue.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: A worker takes about eight minutes to generate embeddings for one Service Bus message. Messages are being processed two or three times each. What is the cause?

options.text: The message lock expires during processing
The queue has duplicate detection disabled
The receiver is using ReceiveAndDelete mode
The queue is partitioned across multiple message stores

explanation: The PeekLock lock duration can be at most five minutes. Eight minutes of processing means the lock lapses, the broker makes the message available again, and another receiver picks it up. Renew the lock during processing, or hand the work off so the handler returns quickly.

whyWrong.B: Duplicate detection prevents the same MessageId being enqueued twice. Here one message is being delivered repeatedly, which is a different problem.
whyWrong.C: ReceiveAndDelete removes the message on receipt, so it could never be delivered again.
whyWrong.D: Partitioning distributes messages for throughput; it does not duplicate deliveries.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: Documents belonging to one customer must be processed strictly in the order they were sent, while different customers can be processed in parallel. What do you use?

options.text: Service Bus sessions, with the customer id as the `SessionId`
A partitioned queue with the customer id as the partition key
A topic with one subscription per customer
Duplicate detection with the customer id as `MessageId`

explanation: Sessions give FIFO ordering within a session. Setting `SessionId` to the customer id means one receiver holds that session and processes its messages in order, while other sessions are handled concurrently by other receivers.

whyWrong.B: Partitioning improves throughput but does not guarantee ordering within a partition key for consumers.
whyWrong.C: A subscription per customer does not scale and still gives no ordering guarantee within a subscription.
whyWrong.D: Duplicate detection suppresses repeats; it says nothing about order, and reusing the customer id as MessageId would discard most messages.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: Duplicate detection is enabled on a queue with a ten-minute window, but duplicates still arrive. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: The sender does not set `MessageId`
The duplicate detection window is shorter than the message TTL
The queue is not in the Premium tier
Sessions are not enabled on the queue

explanation: Duplicate detection compares the `MessageId` of incoming messages within the window. If the sender leaves it unset, the client generates a fresh id per send and nothing ever matches.

whyWrong.B: TTL governs how long a message stays queued and is unrelated to the detection window.
whyWrong.C: Duplicate detection is available on Standard as well as Premium.
whyWrong.D: Sessions provide ordering, not duplicate suppression.

hint: Duplicate detection has to compare something. Ask what field the broker hashes, and whether your sender is setting it.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: A topic has three subscriptions. One of them must receive only messages whose Priority application property equals high. Which filter type is the most efficient?

options.text: A correlation filter matching Priority = high
A SQL filter with the expression Priority = 'high'
A boolean filter set to true, with the check in the receiver
An auto-forward rule to a second topic

explanation: Correlation filters match exact values on system and user properties and are optimised for that case, so they cost less to evaluate than a SQL filter. A SQL filter would also work but is unnecessary when the condition is a simple equality.

whyWrong.B: Functionally correct but more expensive to evaluate than a correlation filter for a plain equality.
whyWrong.C: A true filter delivers everything and moves the work into your receiver, which wastes throughput.
whyWrong.D: Auto-forwarding chains entities together; it does not filter.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: Your pipeline must move 10 MB documents through Service Bus. Which is the appropriate design?

options.text: Store the document in Blob Storage and send the URI
Send the document as the message body on a Standard tier queue
Split the document across 40 messages and reassemble them in the receiver
Base64-encode the document to reduce its size

explanation: The claim check pattern keeps the payload in storage and the pointer in the message. It works on any tier, keeps messages small and fast, and avoids paying broker throughput for bulk bytes.

whyWrong.B: Basic and Standard cap messages at 256 KB, so a 10 MB body is rejected. Premium defaults to 1 MB and can be raised to 100 MB over AMQP, but a broker is still the wrong place for bulk data.
whyWrong.C: Manual chunking adds ordering, correlation and partial-failure problems you would have to solve yourself.
whyWrong.D: Base64 increases size by roughly a third.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: A dead-letter queue has accumulated failed messages that must be inspected and reprocessed. How do you read them?

options.text: Receive from the sub-queue path <queue>/$DeadLetterQueue
Call PeekMessagesAsync on the main queue with a dead-letter filter
Enable dead-letter forwarding, which is the only way to access them
Query the Service Bus namespace metrics API

explanation: The dead-letter queue is a sub-queue addressed as <queue>/$DeadLetterQueue (or <topic>/Subscriptions/<sub>/$DeadLetterQueue). You receive from it with a normal receiver and can resubmit messages to the main queue.

whyWrong.B: Dead-lettered messages are no longer in the main queue, so no filter there can reach them.
whyWrong.C: Forwarding is an optional convenience, not the only access path.
whyWrong.D: Metrics report the count of dead-lettered messages, not their content.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: Throughput on a Service Bus consumer is far below what the queue can deliver, and the worker's CPU is mostly idle. Which processor settings should you look at first?

options.text: `MaxConcurrentCalls` and `PrefetchCount`
`MaxDeliveryCount` and LockDuration
AutoDeleteOnIdle and DefaultMessageTimeToLive
EnablePartitioning and EnableBatchedOperations

explanation: `MaxConcurrentCalls` sets how many messages the processor handles in parallel, and `PrefetchCount` buys down per-message latency by fetching ahead. An idle CPU with a backlog is the signature of both being too low.

whyWrong.B: These govern retry and lock behaviour, not consumption rate.
whyWrong.C: These are entity lifetime settings.
whyWrong.D: Partitioning is set at entity creation and is a broker-side capacity feature, not a consumer tuning knob.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: An Event Grid subscription delivers to a webhook that was down for two days. After it recovers, none of the missed events arrive and there is no record of them. What was not configured?

options.text: No dead-letter destination on the subscription
A longer maximum delivery attempt count
The CloudEvents 1.0 schema on the subscription
An advanced filter matching the event type

explanation: Event Grid retries with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours and 30 attempts by default. Once that is exhausted the event is discarded unless a dead-letter blob container is configured — dead-lettering is opt-in.

whyWrong.B: More attempts within the same 24-hour TTL would not have survived a two-day outage.
whyWrong.C: The schema affects payload shape, not durability.
whyWrong.D: Filters decide which events are sent, not what happens when delivery fails.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: You register a custom webhook as an Event Grid handler. Creation of the subscription fails validation. What must the endpoint do?

options.text: Echo the validationCode from the validation event
Present a certificate issued by a Microsoft-trusted certificate authority
Return HTTP 202 to every request within 100 milliseconds
Register a service principal with the Event Grid Contributor role

explanation: Event Grid proves that you control the endpoint before sending it events. The endpoint must echo the validationCode in its response, or call the validationUrl from the validation event. Azure-native handlers such as Functions with the Event Grid trigger handle this automatically.

whyWrong.B: HTTPS is required, but certificate issuance is not what the handshake checks.
whyWrong.C: Response time matters for delivery, not for subscription creation.
whyWrong.D: RBAC governs who may create the subscription, not endpoint ownership.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: An Event Grid handler occasionally processes the same blob twice, producing duplicate embeddings. What is the correct response?

options.text: Make the handler idempotent on event id
Set the maximum delivery attempts to 1 so events are never retried
Switch the subscription to the CloudEvents schema, which deduplicates events
Enable sessions on the Event Grid topic

explanation: Event Grid delivers at least once, so duplicates are expected behaviour, not a fault. Handlers should key on the event id or the resulting record and make repeat processing a no-op.

whyWrong.B: Setting attempts to 1 turns every transient failure into permanent data loss.
whyWrong.C: The schema changes the envelope format. It has no deduplication semantics.
whyWrong.D: Event Grid topics do not have sessions; that is a Service Bus feature.

hint: Redelivery is part of the contract this service offers, not a defect in it. Given that, ask what the handler has to be able to survive.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: A Function is triggered by Event Grid on every blob created in a storage account, but must only run for PDFs in the incoming/ folder. Where should the filtering happen?

options.text: On the subscription, with subject begins-with and ends-with
In the Function body, returning early for non-matching blobs
On the storage account, with a lifecycle management rule
In a Logic App placed between Event Grid and the Function

explanation: Subject prefix and suffix filters are evaluated by Event Grid before delivery, so unwanted events never reach the Function. That means no invocations to pay for and no wasted cold starts.

whyWrong.B: The Function still gets invoked and billed for every blob in the account.
whyWrong.C: Lifecycle management moves and deletes blobs; it does not filter event delivery.
whyWrong.D: This adds a component and cost to do what the subscription already does natively.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: Match the service to the scenario: millions of telemetry records per hour from inference nodes, needing replay for a downstream analytics job.

options.text: Azure Event Hubs
Azure Event Grid
Azure Service Bus queues
Azure Storage queues

explanation: Event Hubs is the high-throughput streaming ingestion service. Its partitioned log retains events for a configured period, so consumers can replay from an earlier offset — which is exactly the replay requirement.

whyWrong.B: Event Grid distributes discrete reactive notifications and has no retention or replay from an offset.
whyWrong.C: Service Bus is for ordered, transactional business messages; a message is gone once completed.
whyWrong.D: Storage queues are a simple, low-feature queue with no streaming or replay semantics.

hint: Millions per hour plus replay for a later job. That combination points at a streaming service with a retention window, not a queue or a notification router.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: A subscription must only receive events where the data payload's confidence field is above 0.9. Which Event Grid feature supports this?

options.text: An advanced filter using NumberGreaterThan
A subject filter with begins-with confidence
A SQL filter defined on the subscription
An event type filter on the subscription

explanation: Advanced filters evaluate operators such as NumberGreaterThan, StringContains and BoolEquals against fields in the event, including nested paths inside data.

whyWrong.B: Subject filters do string prefix and suffix matching only, and the subject is not the payload.
whyWrong.C: SQL filters belong to Service Bus subscriptions, not Event Grid.
whyWrong.D: Event type filtering selects by type name and cannot inspect field values.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: You need a document-ingestion pipeline where a blob upload triggers embedding generation, and the work must survive a downstream outage of several hours with guaranteed processing. Which design is best?

options.text: Event Grid on blob created, into a Service Bus queue
Event Grid on blob created, delivering directly to the worker's HTTP endpoint
A timer-triggered Function that lists the container every minute
Event Hubs capture writing back into the same storage account

explanation: Event Grid reacts to the blob event; Service Bus provides the durable buffer with retries, dead-lettering and back-pressure. Combining reactive notification with a queue is the standard resilient ingestion pattern.

whyWrong.B: Direct HTTP delivery is limited by Event Grid's 24-hour retry window and gives no back-pressure control.
whyWrong.C: Polling adds latency, costs invocations, and needs its own bookkeeping of what has been processed.
whyWrong.D: Event Hubs Capture writes streaming data to storage — the wrong direction for this scenario.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: A Function on the Consumption plan processes a large document and is terminated after ten minutes. Which change resolves this with the least redesign?

options.text: Move to a Premium or Flex Consumption plan
Increase `functionTimeout` in `host.json` to 30 minutes
Set the HTTP trigger's `authLevel` to admin
Enable Always On in the app settings

explanation: Consumption caps execution at ten minutes and that cap cannot be raised. Premium and Flex Consumption default to 30 minutes and allow more. Splitting the work with Durable Functions is the alternative when you must stay on Consumption.

whyWrong.B: host.json can only set a timeout within the plan's limit. On Consumption the ceiling is still ten minutes.
whyWrong.C: Auth level controls who can call the function.
whyWrong.D: Always On applies to dedicated App Service plans and addresses idle shutdown, not execution length.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: Which NCRONTAB expression runs a timer-triggered Function every five minutes?
explanation: Azure Functions NCRONTAB has six fields and starts with seconds: {second} {minute} {hour} {day} {month} {day-of-week}. '0 */5 * * * *' fires at second zero of every fifth minute.

whyWrong.B: Five fields is standard Linux cron. Functions expects six, so this is misinterpreted.
whyWrong.C: This puts */5 in the seconds field, running every five seconds.
whyWrong.D: This runs every five hours, at minute zero.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: A Function app must read from Service Bus using a managed identity rather than a connection string. The binding's connection property is set to ServiceBusConn. Which app setting is required?

options.text: ServiceBusConn__fullyQualifiedNamespace = sb.windows.net
ServiceBusConn = contoso.servicebus.windows.net
ServiceBusConn__connectionString = Endpoint=sb://...
AzureWebJobsServiceBus = contoso.servicebus.windows.net

explanation: Identity-based connections use a settings prefix with a typed suffix — __fullyQualifiedNamespace for Service Bus, __serviceUri or __accountName for storage, __accountEndpoint for Cosmos DB. The identity also needs the matching data-plane role, such as Azure Service Bus Data Receiver.

whyWrong.B: A bare value in the setting is interpreted as a connection string and will fail to parse.
whyWrong.C: That is the connection-string form, which is what the requirement replaces.
whyWrong.D: This is the wrong setting name, and it is still connection-string shaped.

hint: For identity-based bindings the connection name becomes a prefix, and you supply the resource's address rather than a key. Note the double underscore.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: Which statements about Azure Functions triggers and bindings are correct? Choose two.

options.text: A function has exactly one trigger
A function can have multiple input and output bindings
A function can have multiple triggers if they are of different types
Output bindings must be of the same type as the trigger
Bindings are only available in the in-process .NET model

explanation: Exactly one trigger starts a function; input and output bindings are optional and can be combined freely. A Service Bus trigger writing to Cosmos DB and Blob Storage in the same function is normal.

whyWrong.C: Multiple triggers are not supported. Write separate functions that share a helper.
whyWrong.D: There is no such constraint — mixing binding types is the point.
whyWrong.E: Bindings are fully supported in the isolated worker model, which is the current .NET model.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: A Durable Functions orchestrator stamps each run with a timestamp using DateTime.UtcNow. The timestamps change between replays and downstream records are inconsistent. What is the fix?

options.text: Use context.`CurrentUtcDateTime` in the orchestrator
Cache the timestamp in a static field on the orchestrator class
Store the timestamp in an app setting at deployment time
Set the orchestrator's retry policy to a single attempt

explanation: Orchestrator code is replayed from its event history, so anything non-deterministic — the clock, random numbers, GUIDs, I/O — produces different values on each replay. `CurrentUtcDateTime` is the deterministic clock the framework provides.

whyWrong.B: Static state does not survive across instances or replays, and introduces cross-instance bleed.
whyWrong.C: A deployment-time constant is not the execution time.
whyWrong.D: Retry policy does not prevent replay, which is intrinsic to how orchestrations resume.

hint: An orchestrator re-executes its own code from the top on every replay. Anything reading the real clock will therefore change - you need the value the framework replays.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: A pipeline must chunk a document, embed each chunk in parallel, then write a single summary once all embeddings finish. Which Durable Functions pattern is this?

options.text: Fan-out/fan-in
Function chaining
Monitor
Human interaction

explanation: Fan-out/fan-in starts many activity functions in parallel and awaits them all — typically Task.WhenAll over the task list — before continuing with the aggregate step.

whyWrong.B: Chaining runs steps strictly one after another, which loses the parallelism.
whyWrong.C: The monitor pattern polls a resource until a condition is met.
whyWrong.D: Human interaction waits on an external event such as an approval.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: An HTTP-triggered Function must be callable only by holders of a key that can be revoked independently of other functions in the app. Which `authLevel` do you set?

options.text: function
anonymous
admin
user

explanation: The function level accepts a function-specific key, which can be rotated or revoked without affecting other functions. Host keys also work at this level but apply app-wide.

whyWrong.B: Anonymous requires no key at all.
whyWrong.C: Admin requires the master key, which grants access to everything in the app — the opposite of independent revocation.
whyWrong.D: There is no user auth level; user identity comes from App Service authentication or a gateway.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: Which file holds settings used only when running Functions locally, and is not deployed to Azure?

options.text: `local.settings.json`
`host.json`
`function.json`
`appsettings.json`

explanation: `local.settings.json` holds local connection strings and app settings for the Core Tools. It is excluded from deployment by default, which is why the equivalent values must exist as app settings in Azure.

whyWrong.B: host.json configures the Functions host — retries, batch sizes, logging — and is deployed.
whyWrong.C: function.json describes bindings for a function in script languages and is deployed.
whyWrong.D: appsettings.json is an ASP.NET Core convention, not the Functions local settings file.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: A Function app must reach a private Azure OpenAI endpoint over a virtual network, and must not suffer cold starts on the first request of the morning. Which hosting plan meets both requirements at the lowest cost?

options.text: Premium (Elastic Premium) with pre-warmed instances
Consumption plan with Always On enabled
Dedicated App Service plan on the Free tier
Flex Consumption with minimum instances set to zero

explanation: The Premium plan provides both VNet integration and pre-warmed instances that eliminate cold start, which is exactly the pair of requirements here.

whyWrong.B: Consumption supports neither Always On nor VNet integration.
whyWrong.C: The Free tier has no VNet integration and severe quotas.
whyWrong.D: Flex Consumption supports VNet integration, but zero always-ready instances leaves the cold start in place.

hint: Two requirements at once: private networking and no cold start. Only one hosting plan gives you both.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: Which app setting makes a Function app run from a deployment package, giving atomic deployments and a read-only file system?

options.text: `WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE` = 1
`FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME` = dotnet-isolated
`WEBSITE_NODE_DEFAULT_VERSION` = 20
AzureWebJobsStorage = DefaultEndpointsProtocol=...

explanation: Run-from-package mounts the deployment zip as the app content, so a deployment either fully succeeds or does not take effect. It also removes file-lock issues during deployment.

whyWrong.B: This selects the language worker.
whyWrong.C: This pins a Node version.
whyWrong.D: This is the storage account the Functions host requires for its own state, unrelated to packaging.

docs.title: Run your functions from a package

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: A Service Bus-triggered Function throws on a poison message and the message is retried forever, blocking the queue. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Let it fail and monitor the dead-letter queue
Catch every exception and complete the message so the queue keeps moving
Set `MaxDeliveryCount` to 1 so failures are never retried
Disable the Function until the message is manually deleted

explanation: The delivery-count mechanism exists for exactly this case. After `MaxDeliveryCount` failed attempts the broker moves the message to the dead-letter queue, unblocking the main queue while preserving the message for inspection. 'Retried forever' means the count is set unusually high.

whyWrong.B: Swallowing exceptions destroys the message and hides the failure — the data is simply lost.
whyWrong.C: One attempt means a single transient blip permanently dead-letters good messages.
whyWrong.D: Manual intervention does not scale and stops all processing, not just the bad message.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: Where do you configure the number of messages a Service Bus-triggered Function processes concurrently?

options.text: In `host.json` under extensions.serviceBus
In `local.settings.json` for the app
As an attribute parameter on the trigger
In the Service Bus queue's own properties

explanation: `host.json` holds host-wide extension configuration, including maxConcurrentCalls, prefetchCount and maxAutoLockRenewalDuration for the Service Bus extension.

whyWrong.B: local.settings.json holds local app settings and is not deployed.
whyWrong.C: The trigger attribute names the queue, subscription and connection — not concurrency.
whyWrong.D: Queue properties are broker-side settings such as lock duration and delivery count.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: A Function must write to Cosmos DB after processing a queue message, with the least amount of code. What do you use?

options.text: A Cosmos DB output binding on the function
A `CosmosClient` constructed inside the function body per invocation
A second function triggered by the first over HTTP
A Cosmos DB input binding

explanation: An output binding lets the runtime handle the client lifetime and the write, so the function just returns the object to persist.

whyWrong.B: Constructing a client per invocation is both more code and a performance anti-pattern — if you do use the SDK directly, hold the client in a static or injected singleton.
whyWrong.C: An extra hop adds latency and failure modes for no benefit.
whyWrong.D: An input binding reads from Cosmos DB; this scenario writes.

objective: Develop and implement Azure Functions
stem: A long-running embedding job is started from an HTTP request. The client must get an immediate response and a URL to poll for status. Which Durable Functions pattern applies?

options.text: Async HTTP API with a status endpoint
Aggregator, using a durable entity
Monitor, polling an external resource
Function chaining with activity calls

explanation: The async HTTP API pattern starts an orchestration and immediately returns 202 with a statusQueryGetUri. The client polls that URL until the orchestration completes.

whyWrong.B: Aggregators accumulate state across events over time, which is not the request/poll shape here.
whyWrong.C: The monitor pattern has the orchestration polling something else, not the client polling it.
whyWrong.D: Chaining describes sequential activities inside the orchestration, not the client interaction.

hint: The client cannot wait, so the first response must carry a way to check back later. Durable Functions has a named pattern for exactly that shape.

objective: Develop event- and message-based AI solutions
stem: Documents must be re-embedded at 02:00 tomorrow, not immediately. Which Service Bus feature delivers this without an external scheduler?

options.text: Set `ScheduledEnqueueTime` when sending
Set the message TTL to the delay period
Defer the message when it is received
Send to a topic with a time-based SQL filter

explanation: Scheduled messages sit invisible in the entity until the enqueue time arrives, at which point they become available to receivers. No external timer is needed, and the schedule can be cancelled by sequence number.

whyWrong.B: TTL controls when a message expires, not when it appears.
whyWrong.C: Deferral requires the receiver to have already received the message and to remember its sequence number.
whyWrong.D: Filters are evaluated at enqueue time and cannot delay delivery.
